issues.description: The manuscript states that it uses social learning theory, but the process actually described and tested is the stressor-emotion model of CWB. No observational learning or modeling variables are measured. This theoretical conflation weakens construct-to-theory alignment and makes the hypotheses appear grounded in a framework that is not actually operationalized.
issues.quote: "To understand how incivility experiences from customers may be impacting employee affect and behavior over time, we utilize social learning theory (Bandura, 1977)... Applied to enacted incivility, the general premise of the model suggests that enacted incivility occurs due to a sequence of events where environmental stressors at work lead to enacted incivility through appraisal, perceptions of the stressor, and negative emotions (Spector & Fox, 2005)."

issues.description: The serial mediation claim is not temporally identified because the second mediator (compassion fatigue) and the outcome (enacted incivility) are both measured at T4. This means the model cannot establish that compassion fatigue preceded enacted incivility, undermining the claimed temporal sequence for Hypothesis 4.
issues.quote: "T4 Compassion Fatigue" ... "Enacted Incivility (T4)"

issues.description: The lagged regressions do not control for prior levels of the mediator or outcome variables (e.g., prior negative emotions, prior compassion fatigue, prior enacted incivility). As a result, the analyses do not test change over time and cannot rule out stable between-person differences as the source of the observed associations.
issues.quote: "We tested this hypothesis by regressing negative emotions toward patients (T3) onto experienced patient incivility (T2)."

issues.description: The manuscript incorrectly describes the serial indirect effect for Hypothesis 4 as the product of only two paths (a × d). A serial mediation from experienced incivility to enacted incivility through negative emotions and compassion fatigue requires multiplying three constituent paths, not two. This is a substantive reporting/statistical error in the model description.
issues.quote: "Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d)."

issues.description: The participant counts do not reconcile. If 450 responded at T4 and 78 were excluded for data quality, that yields 372. The additional claim that 16 were excluded for missing time points is inconsistent with the reported final N. Because participants who missed a wave were not invited forward, T4 respondents should already be complete cases. This inconsistency raises concern about how the analytic sample was formed.
issues.quote: "n = 450 responded at time 4" / "Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points)... were included in the final sample." / "This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372."

issues.description: The reported final sample is N = 372, but Table 1 and Table 2 use N = 321, and Table 3 uses N = 244. The moderator missingness explains only part of the loss, but the manuscript does not explain why 51 cases disappear from the main mediation analyses. This unexplained case loss prevents evaluation of bias and reproducibility.
issues.quote: "This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372." / "Note. N = 321." / "Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable."

issues.description: The design forced nonresponse to become permanent attrition because participants missing any wave were not invited to later waves, and only completers were analyzed. This creates a potentially nonrandom, highly selected analytic sample and can bias longitudinal estimates.
issues.quote: "Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys" and "Only participants who completed all four surveys... were included in the final sample."

issues.description: The attrition check is not a formal analysis. It compares only T1-only respondents to completers, does not address those who dropped out after T2 or T3, and uses a vague heuristic ('within one standard deviation') rather than statistical tests or missing-data diagnostics. This is insufficient to support an assumption of ignorable attrition.
issues.quote: "Participants who responded only to the T1 survey reported similar demographic information compared to those who completed all four time periods and had scale values on the key study constructs within one standard deviation of the means for the final sample..."

issues.description: The manuscript states that 78 participants were excluded for poor data quality, but the enumerated reasons account for only 57 cases (56 inconsistent demographics + 1 missing >50% of questions). The remaining exclusions are unexplained, and 'reasonably consistent' is not operationalized. This makes the exclusion process nontransparent and nonreplicable.
issues.quote: "n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality" ... "(a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods (n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age); or (b) missing values exceeded 50% of the questions (n = 1)."

issues.description: Patient acuity is measured with a single self-reported percentage of patients deemed 'severe,' anchored to whatever departmental scale the respondent happens to use. Because departments use different instruments and thresholds, the resulting measure is not a common metric across participants. Reliability is unreported and likely low for a single item. The item also conflates acuity with workload and case mix.
issues.quote: "we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were 'severe'" and "Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools"

issues.description: Nearly half of missing acuity responses were outside the expected numerical range, indicating respondents did not clearly understand how to answer the item (e.g., percentage vs proportion). This is direct evidence of measurement confusion and threatens the validity of the moderator.
issues.quote: "For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response)."

issues.description: The predictor combines incivility from patients and family/friends, but the mediator measures negative emotions only toward patients. If the uncivil source is a family member, the mediator does not match the source of the experience. This weakens the proposed mechanism and creates ambiguity about what interpersonal target the emotion construct represents.
issues.quote: Experienced incivility prompt: "how often have you been in a situation where any of your patients or patient family members/friends..." / Negative emotions prompt: "How often do you feel the following emotions towards patients"

issues.description: The enacted incivility scale is adapted from a generic workplace incivility measure, but some items may reflect routine clinical judgment or workflow constraints rather than rudeness in nurse-patient interactions. The fact that 90% of pilot respondents reported engaging in these behaviors suggests the adapted items may be capturing normative care interactions rather than uncivil conduct.
issues.quote: "Doubted one or more patient’s/patient family members’ judgment on a matter over which they had responsibility" and "90% of respondents indicated that they personally had engaged in these behaviors towards patients or their families."

issues.description: The manuscript treats compassion fatigue as an exhaustion mechanism triggered by incivility, but the construct as defined and measured includes secondary trauma from exposure to patients' suffering. That component is conceptually distinct from strain caused by patient rudeness. This makes the mediator broader than the proposed mechanism and may introduce variance unrelated to incivility.
issues.quote: "Compassion fatigue consists of burnout and secondary trauma components" and example item: "I am losing sleep over a patient’s traumatic experiences."

issues.description: The manuscript claims acceptable discriminant validity, yet the reported intercorrelations between supposedly distinct constructs are extraordinarily high (up to .96). Correlations of this magnitude strongly suggest overlap, shared method variance, or lack of distinctiveness among negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility.
issues.quote: "The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable" / Table 1 values include "T3 Negative Emotions ... .91", "T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .96", and "T4 Enacted Incivility ... .94"

issues.description: The model includes highly correlated predictors/mediators simultaneously, yet there is no discussion of multicollinearity diagnostics. With cross-construct correlations around .91-.96 and R² = .81 for enacted incivility, coefficient estimates are likely unstable, which undermines interpretation of specific indirect paths and relative importance comparisons.
issues.quote: Table 1 reports correlations as high as ".96" and Table 2 reports "R2 ... .81" for enacted incivility.

issues.description: The discussion of coefficient magnitudes is numerically inconsistent with the reported regression results. The manuscript says the compassion-fatigue coefficient is 'nearly six times' the negative-emotions coefficient, but Table 2 shows .57 vs .28 (about 2x), and the supplemental regression reports both as .23. The later claim that compassion fatigue is the 'stronger driver' is therefore not well supported.
issues.quote: "the last step of the simple mediation reflects a parameter estimate for compassion fatigue that is nearly six times that of negative emotions" / Table 2: "T3 Negative Emotions ... .28**" and "T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .57***" / supplemental regression: "negative emotions (B = .23...); and compassion fatigue (B = .23...)"

issues.description: The discussion states that the study found 'partial mediation,' but the direct path from experienced incivility to enacted incivility in Table 2 is non-significant. That pattern is not evidence of partial mediation for the focal outcome path and should not be described that way without clarification.
issues.quote: "Our results support a partial mediation process" / Table 2: "T2 Customer Incivility ... Enacted Incivility (T4) ... -.07 ... -1.14"

issues.description: Participants were recruited through open flyers, personal networks, social media, and forums, and eligibility appears to have been checked only by self-report. No licensure, employment, or hospital affiliation verification is described. This is a meaningful design weakness for a specialized professional sample, especially given the notable data-quality exclusions.
issues.quote: "participants initiated the contact and study procedures by clicking on the study link or QR code" and "To help ensure that the participants were from healthcare contexts, we highlighted the nursing focus in the recruitment and consent information and directly asked participants if they met the inclusion criteria."

issues.description: The inclusion criteria described in recruitment materials specify full-time nurses in high-stakes/critical care settings, but the final sample description includes part-time nurses and only requires working more than one shift per week. This unreported shift in eligibility criteria affects interpretability and comparability of the sample.
issues.quote: Recruitment materials listed inclusion criteria as "working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting as a nurse" but the final sample description states "All participants were currently employed as a nurse (part- or full-time), worked more than one shift a week".

issues.description: Because the total number of eligible nurses reached is unknown, no response rate can be calculated and representativeness cannot be evaluated. This is a basic reporting gap for interpreting external validity.
issues.quote: "Although the full population size that was sampled from is unknown"

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly makes causal claims that are too strong for an observational self-report panel, especially given same-wave links, omitted autoregressive controls, and likely stable person-level confounds. Temporal ordering alone does not justify statements that the predictor 'leads to' the outcomes.
issues.quote: "This method also supports a lower likelihood of third variable effects ... and allows for stronger causal inferences" and "These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility."

issues.description: The core interpretation is that experienced incivility spreads to future customers generally, but the study cannot distinguish whether enacted incivility was aimed at different patients/families or at the same prior perpetrators. The authors acknowledge this limitation, meaning the headline 'incivility begets incivility' spillover claim is not directly tested.
issues.quote: "another limitation to the longitudinal design of this study is the chance that an employee may continue an uncivil relationship with certain patients across various time points (i.e., via retribution pathways). Our theoretical framework and hypotheses did not incorporate interpersonal relationships and may not be reflective of direct experienced-enacted relationships if they existed."

issues.description: The discussion generalizes the findings to service industries and customer settings broadly, despite a specialized U.S. high-stakes nursing sample that is overwhelmingly female and embedded in unique care dynamics. The data do not warrant broad claims about employee-customer relationships generally.
issues.quote: "This adds to the generalizability of prior customer incivility research to further support that experiencing incivility from customers – even when the customers are patients... – is associated with detrimental employee and customer outcomes over time."

issues.description: The manuscript reports only a single four-factor CFA, omits the details of the alternative models it says were tested, and does not test longitudinal measurement invariance across waves despite using repeated adapted/shortened scales. Without invariance evidence, it is unclear whether the same constructs are being measured equivalently over time.
issues.quote: "First, we assessed our hypothesized four-factor model absent of the temporal control measures... The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable ... and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors."

issues.description: All variables were measured at each wave, but only selected waves were used for the focal hypothesis tests, leaving many possible lag structures and model specifications. The manuscript also adds 'unhypothesized' supplemental analyses after the primary tests. This degree of analytic flexibility increases the risk that results depend on researcher choices rather than a uniquely specified model.
issues.quote: "The subsequent waves were included for hypothesis testing (see Figure 1 for information what measurement period each variable in the model was taken from)." and "We conducted a series of supplemental analyses to 1) address unhypothesized moderation effects and 2) investigate the relationship between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility."

issues.description: Participants were recruited from multiple hospitals and likely from different units/departments, yet the analyses treat all observations as independent. Shared hospital or unit norms, staffing levels, and patient populations could induce clustering and confounding, but no cluster structure or adjustment is reported.
issues.quote: "Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S."

issues.description: All focal constructs—experienced incivility, negative emotions, compassion fatigue, enacted incivility, and patient acuity—come from the same respondent, using self-report questionnaires. This raises substantial same-source/common-method concerns, especially because some key constructs are measured in the same wave and the intercorrelations are extremely high.
issues.quote: "First, our data were collected using self-report questionnaires."
